concept: RichTextEditor is a note field that lets a person bold a word, link an address or make a list. It is the Textarea well with a row of round keys printed above it, so the writing stays in a recess and the formatting stays on keys you can press. Its output is a small, whitelisted piece of HTML, the way a label printer accepts only the marks it can print.

default_to_avoid.pattern: rich text editor shown as a white page with a grey toolbar strip of tiny icon buttons glued to the top edge
default_to_avoid.why_not: Tiny glued icons fall below the 44px hit area and make the field and its tools one pale panel; here the keys are separate parts and the writing sits in its own recess.

references.source: system/FORM.md input class: recessed well, full width of its column, label printed above on the inset line
Braun ET 66 calculator (Dietrich Lubs, 1987): a row of round keys above the entry window, each key one function
WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: toolbar pattern with one tab stop and arrow-key movement between the keys

derivation.consequence: the window is recessed into the body (inverse light)
derivation.form: The writing area is the same recessed well as Input and Textarea, so formatted text reads as written into the body and the keys above stay raised.

derivation.consequence: every part keeps ≥44px hit area even when it draws smaller
derivation.form: Each formatting key is a 44px round IconButton, so a thumb finds Bold or Link without the tiny glued icons of a typical editor bar.

derivation.consequence: every mechanism has its keyboard map
derivation.form: The toolbar is one tab stop; arrows, Home and End walk the keys, and Ctrl or Command with B, I and K work inside the writing area.

derivation.consequence: glass appears on caps, lamps, latched keys and chips only
derivation.form: A format that is on, such as bold at the caret, latches its key as frosted glass through IconButton, and nothing else in the editor is glass.

derivation.consequence: labels sit on the body's inset line
derivation.form: The printed label, the keys, the well and the messages stack in one column on the inset line.

options.name: round keys in a row above the well
legend words docked inside the well under a seam
capsule key column at the inline-end side

variants.reason: A keeps the well a pure Input-family recess and uses the 44px latched round key dial already has, so the on state is a real shape change. B puts text-height words inside the well, which blurs where writing ends and tools begin, and its underline is the only cue. C takes 56px of width from the well, which is the scarce thing on a phone.

root.why: The field stacks label, keys, well and messages in one column so everything sits on the inset line and the layout does not reflow between states.

label.why: The printed name uses the label size in medium weight like the printing beside every other part, and it names the writing area for assistive tech.

bar.why: The row of keys is one toolbar with a single tab stop and arrow-key movement, so a keyboard user does not tab through six keys to reach the text.

well.why: The recess takes the inverse light, shade on its top-left inner edge, so the person sees where text goes.

field.why: Typed text is primary ink on the sunken plastic at more than 4.5:1, with a line box tall enough for Thai marks, and links are underlined ink, never orange.

linkRow.why: The address is asked in an Input well that appears under the keys, so a link is typed in a real field with its own label rather than a browser prompt.

linkKeys.why: Apply, Remove and Cancel are 44px keys in one row beside the address, wrapping under it on a narrow phone.

hint.why: The hint is secondary ink in the caption size under the well.

error.why: The error is critical red with a glyph and words, never orange and never colour alone.

glyph.why: A printed mark beside the words means invalid is never told by colour alone, for people who cannot see the red.

focus-within.why: The well shows the same dark ring as every part when the writing area holds the keyboard focus.

data-empty=true.why: An empty area prints its prompt in secondary ink so the person knows where to write, and the prompt disappears with the first character.

data-invalid=true.why: An invalid well draws its edge in the critical red, which is never orange, and the message below names the problem.

data-disabled=true.why: A disabled editor loses its recess shadow and fades, so it reads as not taking input right now.

data-readonly=true.why: A read-only editor keeps full ink and drops the keys, because it is a reading and not an unavailable setting.

@media forced-colors: active.why: In forced colours the well keeps a real border, links keep their underline and the focus ring uses the system highlight colour.
